title: Ex 3.3 #7 (second question) · Passwords mixing upper and lower case
prompt: A password has exactly 5 characters, and each character is a letter of the alphabet in upper or lower case (52 possible characters). How many passwords mix the two cases, using at least one upper-case letter and at least one lower-case letter?
answer_format: A whole number, or an expression for it like 26^4 or binom(10, 3).

mistakes.hint: That removes only the all-lower-case passwords. The all-upper-case ones don't mix the cases either.
That counts every password, including the ones written entirely in one case.
That's the number of single-case passwords: the ones to exclude, not keep.

hints: It's easier to count the passwords that fail: those written in only one case.
There are 26^5 all-lower-case passwords and just as many all-upper-case ones. Remove both groups from the total.
solution: With 52 characters available there are $52^5 = 380{,}204{,}032$ passwords in all.
A password fails to mix cases exactly when it is all lower case ($26^5$ of them) or all upper case (another $26^5$). These groups don't overlap, so $2 \cdot 26^5 = 23{,}762{,}752$ passwords fail.

reference.note: This exact exercise (its second question), restated in ProofLab's words. Uses the subtraction and addition principles (Section 3.3).
